subject: Medicine
summary: Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first detected during pregnancy, driven by placental hormones and insulin resistance. It requires early screening, lifestyle modification, and pharmacologic control to prevent maternal and fetal complications.

sections.p: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is glucose intolerance that begins or is first recognized during pregnancy. Diagnosis is based on an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) performed between 24–28 weeks gestation or earlier if risk factors are present.
b: Screening at 24–28 weeks or earlier for high‑risk women

sections.p: The International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) criteria stage GDM into mild, moderate, or severe based on fasting and post‑load glucose levels. Severity guides treatment intensity.

The primary driver is pregnancy‑induced insulin resistance due to placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol). Secondary factors include obesity, family history of diabetes, and prior GDM.

t.b: Assesses average glucose over 3 months; useful if OGTT unavailable. Elevated HbA1c (>6.5%) suggests pre‑existing diabetes.

sections.p: Most women are asymptomatic. Mild hyperglycaemia may cause increased thirst or urination. Severe cases can present with polyuria, polydipsia, or signs of pre‑eclampsia.
b: Polyuria and polydipsia in severe cases

t.b: Elevated fasting glucose (>5.1 mmol/L) indicates impaired fasting glucose.
A value >11.1 mmol/L in a symptomatic patient supports GDM diagnosis.
A value >6.5% suggests pre‑existing diabetes; <6.5% supports GDM.

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for signs of pre‑eclampsia, severe hyperglycaemia, or fetal distress. Complications include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and future type 2 diabetes.

t.b: Macrosomia or growth restriction suggests poor glycaemic control.

sections.p: First line is dietary counseling and physical activity. If targets are not met, metformin or insulin is added. Metformin is preferred in low‑resource settings due to ease of use; insulin is reserved for severe or uncontrolled cases.

t.b: Improves insulin sensitivity; chosen for oral administration and low cost.
Used when glycaemic targets cannot be achieved with metformin or in severe cases.

sections.p: Weekly glucose monitoring during treatment, with postpartum glucose testing at 6–12 weeks. Prevention focuses on healthy weight, balanced diet, and regular exercise before and during pregnancy.

t.b: Detects persistent diabetes; a positive result indicates need for long‑term management.

sections.p: Type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and pre‑existing diabetes can mimic GDM. Distinguishing features include timing of onset and response to pregnancy‑related insulin resistance.
HbA1c may be falsely low in early pregnancy due to increased red cell turnover. OGTT can be affected by recent meals or illness.

faq.a: Maintaining a healthy weight, balanced diet, and regular exercise before and during pregnancy reduces risk.
Yes, it is considered safe and is preferred in low‑resource settings when insulin is unavailable.

faq.q: Will I develop type 2 diabetes after pregnancy?
faq.a: About 50% of women with GDM develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years; regular follow‑up is essential.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of insulin resistance in pregnancy and how it leads to GDM.
Outline the diagnostic criteria for GDM and describe the management steps if glucose targets are not met.
Discuss the potential complications of untreated GDM for both mother and fetus.
